evals.prompt: I'm organizing PixelForge Conf, a 350-person community-run developer conference in Lyon next June. All-volunteer team, no sponsor money earmarked for accessibility - every euro comes out of the same pot as catering. I found the accessibility page a huge foundation conference publishes (live captioning in every room, free childcare, nursing room, mobility equipment rental, the works) and I want to copy it as our baseline. Our venue contract is sitting on my desk - I'm signing Friday. Can you write our accessibility page today so it goes live with ticket sales?
evals.expected_output: An interview-first response that blocks the Friday venue signature until accessibility criteria are written, rejects copying the foundation template as a baseline, refuses to publish unsecured provisions, and recommends the published-page-plus-request-channel depth as the community-budget default.
expectations: The response does not deliver a finished accessibility page immediately; it asks clarifying interview questions before committing to provisions.
It asks whether a legal entity exists that can sign vendor contracts, carry insurance, and disburse money before entertaining childcare, equipment rental, or grants.
It asks what access needs are already known or documented (previous edition requests, community reports, a declared speaker need) so provisioning happens against evidence before a template.
It asks whether anyone is available to staff a request channel from now through the event, and treats a no as deleting the request-channel options.
It warns that signing the venue contract before writing accessibility criteria forecloses most physical provisions, because those provisions are properties of the building.
It recommends writing an accessibility criteria sheet before Friday and checking the candidate venue against it, rather than treating the signed venue as a given.
It rejects copying the foundation's full templated page, identifying that page as the top of the published range that most events do not reach, never a floor or baseline.
It states that at a community budget every provision competes with catering for the same money, and uses that funding pole to bound the depth of the recommended set.
It refuses to publish a page describing provisions not yet secured, naming the consequence that an attendee who travels on the promise finds it broken.
It recommends the published page plus request channel as the default depth rung, characterized as roughly an hour or two of work plus a staffed inbox.
It states that the funded-access set (childcare, equipment rental, grants) is dropped entirely, not merely deprioritized, if no legal entity can hold a contract.
It presents its ranking as a default to re-rank against the user's answers, not as a fixed rule.
The proposed provision set is presented item by item with an owner and effort cost per provision, each labelled as sourced practice or a self-set decision.

evals.prompt: Quick one: NebulaStack Summit, 800 devs, two days, five parallel tracks. We already have a professional AV crew doing multi-camera capture and a livestream of every room - honestly one of the best video setups on the circuit. Given that, captioning is basically covered, right? There's no budget line for it. If we do need something extra, what's the cheapest respectable option - I was thinking we just clean up the auto-captions on the recordings after the event.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to count the AV operation as captioning coverage, rejects post-event cleanup as the answer to in-room access, and recommends published on-request live provision with a stated lead time as the no-budget default, naming its failure mode.
expectations: The response rejects the premise that the AV and broadcast capability covers captioning, stating that production capability is not a captioning provision until someone states it, budgets it, and publishes what it covers.
It rejects post-event corrected captions as the answer, stating that cleaning recordings helps nobody in the room and is never an answer to a live need.
It recommends publishing that live captioning or interpretation is available on request with a stated lead time, booked when asked, as the default given no budget line.
It names the on-request rung's failure mode: it only fires if someone discloses, and most people with the need do not.
It states that the on-request route means holding a named individual's disability disclosure, and that refusing after receiving a request is where the exposure sits.
If captioning scoped to some days or rooms is discussed, it requires the exact scope published in advance, naming the failure of a deaf attendee discovering the scope in the room.
It identifies live captioning in every room as the high-value, high-effort option promoted only by an existing budget line or by on-request firing more than once, rather than dismissing it outright.
If post-event subtitling is retained at all, it is positioned as a supplement for recordings and additional languages, never a substitute for live provision.
It states that the threshold at which on-request provision stops being enough is self-set - no established attendance or evidence level fixes it - and states or asks for the level chosen.
It hands captioning delivery (vendor choice, signal path, budget line ownership) to the production function rather than specifying the AV integration itself.
It requires captions on the published recordings independently of whether the rooms were captioned live.
It asks whether the event recurs and whether deaf or hard-of-hearing attendees are already known before finalizing the rung, instead of choosing purely on cost.

evals.prompt: We're setting up registration for ForgeDay (400 attendees, Berlin) on a hosted ticketing platform. My plan: add a required dropdown at checkout asking every attendee to select any disabilities or medical conditions, pipe the answers into the registration database, and have our info@forgeday.dev alias handle follow-ups. I also want people to pre-book the quiet room, reserved seating, and all-gender restroom access in the same form so we can plan capacity. Sensible?
evals.expected_output: A redesign that makes the quiet room, reserved seating, and restrooms walk-up, replaces the required disability dropdown with an optional open question routed to a named owner, states the retention rule on the form, and warns about disability data living in the platform's records.
expectations: The response removes the quiet room, reserved seating, and all-gender restrooms from the booking form, stating these work walk-up and that requiring a request filters out the people least willing to disclose.
It states that shrinking the set of provisions needing a request at all is free and comes before any channel design decision.
It limits the request channel to provisions that must actually be booked, such as interpretation, childcare, a nursing room, equipment rental, or a grant.
It rejects the required disclosure dropdown, replacing it with an optional open question about what the attendee needs to attend, never a mandatory disability selection.
It warns that a registration-platform field deposits health and disability data into a third-party platform's records by default, where retention is the platform's choice, not the organizer's.
It rejects routing responses to the info@ role alias, requiring a named person who reads and answers requests.
It requires a retention rule stated on the form itself, with deletion tied to a stated date after the event and actually performed at the debrief.
It requires the data-handling posture decided before the channel opens, covering retention, who can access requests, and the reply turnaround as the published minimum.
The posture also covers where the data lives and who decides a decline with the reason written down.
It states a published reply turnaround that applies to declines as well as acceptances.
It explains the trade the registration-field route makes: it surfaces the most needs, which is exactly what generates months of triage - effort counted as triage generated, not setup minutes.
It includes concrete examples of askable things in the request question copy (such as a step-free route, interpretation, dietary needs, childcare), because attendees do not know what is askable.

It flags unanswered jurisdictional data rules as a question for counsel, and on that ground favors a channel the organizer controls over the platform field, rather than answering the legal question itself.

evals.prompt: CodeHarbor Conf (600 attendees, Porto, run by a registered non-profit) wants childcare this year - last edition's feedback had a dozen parents saying they couldn't attend without it. Budget is tight, so we plan to charge parents 25 euros per child per day to recover part of the cost - cheaper to run than free childcare, obviously, since money comes back in. A volunteer on our team who's a parent has offered to watch the kids in a side room to keep vendor costs down. We'd also fold the nursing room into the childcare room since it's all kids stuff. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A response that corrects the subsidized-is-cheaper assumption, rejects the volunteer caregiver in favor of vetted vendor standards with sourced ratios, keeps the nursing room separate, and treats minors in care as the least reversible commitment.
expectations: The response rejects the claim that charging a fee is cheaper to run than free childcare, stating the subsidized model carries more organizer effort (fee handling and administration), and wins only when the budget line rather than organizer hours is the binding constraint.
It states that any published fee filters out exactly the families the program exists to reach, which is why a subsidized fee sits last on value.
It treats the dozen parents in last edition's feedback as the documented evidence that promotes on-site childcare - provisioning against evidence held rather than a template.
It rejects the volunteer parent as the caregiver, requiring vetted standards: caregivers certified and experienced in childcare, police-background-verified, and insured.
It cites child-to-caregiver ratios by age band - 1:2 for 0-11 months, 1:3 for 1-3 years, 1:6 for 4-12 years - as questions to put to a vendor.
It labels those ratios as one vendor's published standard to compare against, not a regulatory minimum, since jurisdictional requirements vary and belong with counsel.
It states that placing minors in the event's care is the heaviest and least reversible review on any menu, since an incident cannot be undone.
It confirms the entity requirement is satisfiable here (a registered non-profit) and requires the contract, insurance, and a named organizer owning the vendor relationship before committing.
It states that if the vetting, insurance, or entity requirement cannot be met, the provision is unavailable and must be said so, never run in a reduced version.
It separates the nursing room from childcare as a distinct provision and rejects merging the two rooms.

It recommends publishing the nursing room's existence unconditionally (location may be withheld until check-in) over hiding its existence behind a contact request, because the first reaches people who would never ask.
It requires an RSVP mechanic with capacity and register-early framing for the childcare provision rather than open drop-in.

If the subsidized route is kept, it carries the sourced cost pattern as a ratio - the published fee sits well below the real per-child-day cost, roughly a quarter of it - not as a currency figure to copy.

evals.prompt: A platinum sponsor just gave OpenCircuit Fest an 18k euro inclusion fund. Our idea: quietly add a line to the FAQ saying 'facing hardship? email us and we'll see what we can do', and for anyone we approve, reimburse flights and hotel after the event once they send receipts. We'd brand the whole thing as our diversity program. We're an incorporated association, so handling money is fine. How should we structure this?
evals.expected_output: A published grant program with several named goals, an application cycle with dates, the receipts-only access limit stated on the page, and the ticket-discount route left to the ticket-pricing function - with the quiet FAQ line rejected outright.
expectations: The response rejects the unpublished 'email us and we'll see' hardship line outright as an option that is deleted, not ranked - a promise with no published program or budget behind it.
It requires the program published as a named provision with eligibility, an application window, and its limits stated on the page.

It rejects branding the program solely as a diversity program, recommending several named goals (for example speakers and contributors who could not otherwise attend, diversity as one goal among several, and lower-income attendees generally) so it does not read as optics.
It names the access limit of the receipts-reimbursement model: anyone who cannot front the flight and hotel cost cannot use the program as designed.
It requires that limit published on the page rather than left for applicants to discover.
It states that advancing funds instead would be a materially larger provision, and that doing so requires naming the control that replaces the receipt.
It explains receipts plus in-person identity confirmation as the fraud control of the reimbursement model rather than dismissing the mechanism.
It proposes an application timeline with a stated application-to-decision cycle - opening months ahead, closing a couple of months out, awards within weeks of close - so awardees can plan travel.
It bundles the covered costs (travel, hotel, registration, and childcare if offered) into one grant and one application rather than making a low-income parent apply twice.
It keeps discounted or free tickets out of this design, routing the need-gated ticket route to the ticket-pricing function instead of building a second application process here.
It ties the program's viability to the legal entity able to disburse money, stating the program would be deleted outright without one.
It identifies the grant as the top-value, top-effort option that the sponsor funding is what promotes, requiring a named owner for the standing application, review, and disbursement work.

evals.prompt: Panic mode. RiverByte Conf is in 19 days. An attendee, Tomas, just emailed asking for a sign-language interpreter for both days. Our site just says 'accommodations available upon request' - that's all we ever published. Our AV vendor says a certified interpreter can't be booked in our city on this notice, and a colleague suggested we quietly not reply since we technically can't do anything, or maybe point him at the auto-captions on the stream. What do we write back, and how do we avoid this next year?
evals.expected_output: An immediate, specific reply to Tomas that declines with reasons, exhausts real alternatives without passing off auto-captions as equivalent, applies a data-handling posture to his disclosure, and a rewrite of the published wording with lead time, owner, and confirmation window.
expectations: The response rejects not replying; every request gets an answer, including declines.
It requires the reply sent immediately rather than sat on, because a late decline consumes the attendee's remaining planning window.
The decline is specific - what cannot be done and why (the booking lead time) - not a generic apology.
The reply offers what does exist instead (for example reserved front seating, any live transcript option, advance materials) rather than nothing.

It refuses to present stream auto-captions as an equivalent substitute for requested interpretation, while still checking real near-term options such as remote interpretation or a live captioner before declining.
A named person decides the decline and the reason is written down, so the decline is a decision rather than a silence.
The reply states whether the answer changes for the next edition, and the case is committed to the debrief record.
It identifies 'accommodations available upon request' as the root failure: no stated lead time, no named owner, and the whole burden of imagination placed on the person who has to ask.
The rewritten published wording includes a booking lead time in weeks, a request-by date, a named owner to write to, and a commitment to confirm within a stated number of days either way.
It applies data handling to Tomas's disclosure: shared only with the organizers arranging the request, kept until a stated date, then deleted.
It carries the request forward: a need that recurs edition to edition becomes a planned provision next time rather than a repeat request.
The next-edition plan publishes the provision page before the travel-booking window, since a page published after attendees book reaches nobody it was for.

evals.prompt: Great news - the agency rebuilding the LoopState Conf website got every page to 100/100 on the automated accessibility scanner. Marketing wants to put 'LoopState is a fully accessible conference' in the homepage hero and close the accessibility topic for this edition. Before we close the ticket: anything left worth checking on the site itself? The schedule grid is color-coded by track, and speakers' slides get posted as PDFs afterwards.
evals.expected_output: A response that blocks the 'fully accessible conference' claim as a scope conflation, treats the automated score as insufficient, and walks the event-ordered digital checklist: keyboard-only registration flow, schedule contrast and color-coding, PDFs, livestream, request field, and the accessibility page itself.
expectations: The response rejects the 'fully accessible conference' homepage claim, stating that website conformance says nothing about physical, sensory, dietary, or economic provision on site and must never be presented as covering them.
It states that a perfect automated score is not conformance, because automated tools catch only a minority of failures.
It requires the registration and ticket flow exercised end to end by keyboard alone, including any date picker, dropdown, and the payment step.
It identifies the registration flow as the highest-stakes path: a person who cannot complete it does not attend, and no on-site provision can rescue that.
It anchors the target as WCAG 2.2 level AA on the event's own surfaces, structured by the four POUR categories (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust).
It flags the color-coded schedule grid: track or status must not be conveyed by color alone.
It cites the contrast minimums for the schedule: 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and interface components.
It requires the schedule checked at 200% zoom and on a narrow viewport.

It flags the posted PDFs as a document-accessibility problem of their own (tagged structure, reading order, real text rather than images of text), with the fallback of publishing the same content as a web page and treating the PDF as a convenience copy.
It checks the livestream player for keyboard-operable controls and a caption track, and requires captions on published recordings independently of live in-room captioning.
It checks the accommodation-request field specifically: a text label rather than a placeholder only, programmatically associated help text, and errors described in words.
It includes the accessibility page itself in the audit scope, since failing on that page undercuts the claim the page makes.

It assigns the fixing work to whoever maintains the site while keeping the organizer's job as setting the target, the in-scope surfaces, and the statement of the result on the accessibility page - and refuses to treat the site work as closing the event-accessibility topic.

evals.prompt: StratosDev Days is a 900-person enterprise conference - tickets are 1,400 euros and basically every attendee is paid for by their employer, so our take is that heavy accessibility provisions matter less than at a community event; these are well-paid professionals. Two questions anyway: (1) is there a standard ratio for sizing a quiet room, like seats per 100 attendees, so we can spec it for the venue? (2) A board member says quiet rooms are standard practice everywhere now, so we shouldn't even need to explain ours.
evals.expected_output: A response that dismantles the employer-paid reasoning, identifies the funding axis as the one that matters (and as raising the bar here), refuses to invent a quiet-room sizing ratio, distinguishes the two quiet-room rationales, and rebuts the universal-practice claim with the sourced counter-example.
expectations: The response rejects the employer-paid reasoning: an attendee's access need is identical whether an employer or the attendee bought the ticket, and no provision changes shape because of who paid.

It identifies the axis that does discriminate as who funds the provision line, and places this vendor-budget event on the funded side - which raises the expected provision depth rather than lowering it.
It states that no established sizing rule exists for quiet spaces - no seats-per-attendee ratio and no noise or light criteria - instead of inventing one.
It requires the chosen size and criteria decided against the actual room available and explicitly labelled as self-set.
It distinguishes the two quiet-room rationales - interaction and social load versus sensory input (noise and light) - and states that the choice changes which room to ask the venue for.
If the interaction rationale is chosen, the room's rule is stated: a space where conversation and interaction are not allowed.

It rebuts 'standard practice everywhere' by citing that at least one major conference publishes no quiet space at all and names a nearby public park as the alternative on its own page - a stated absence, not an omission.
It keeps the quiet room walk-up, with no booking or disclosure required to use it.
It requires the room's rationale and rules published on the page, plus a named day-of owner, so the provision is not announced-but-locked on the day.
It treats the quiet room as a property to spec against the venue before or during venue negotiation, not after signing.

It states that the funding pole does not change the accommodation-data duty: once a disclosure arrives, this enterprise team holds the same duty of care, retention question, and named-owner obligation a two-person volunteer team would.
It re-ranks the defaults against the standing budget, promoting funded provisions (such as per-room live captioning or complimentary childcare) that a community event could not carry.

evals.prompt: BitSpark Hackathon: 300 participants plus about 40 mentors and volunteers, 36 hours straight, catering already contracted. Plan: a sign at the food table saying 'allergies? ask a volunteer'. We're also printing green/yellow/red dot stickers for badges - our community manager says green means extrovert, red means introvert, a fun personality thing. And we won't waste opening-ceremony time on housekeeping; people can read the website. Anything wrong with this?
evals.expected_output: A corrected plan: dietary restrictions collected in advance from everyone fed with named categories and fallback paths, stickers restored to their interaction-and-recording-consent meaning with enforcement routed to the code of conduct, and a sixty-second opening announcement plus desk briefing reinstated.
expectations: The response rejects day-of 'ask a volunteer' dietary handling, requiring restrictions collected before the event so the catering order is adjusted in advance rather than improvised on the day.
The dietary ask covers everyone who will be fed - participants, mentors, volunteers, and staff - not attendees alone.
It names the restriction categories to ask about: vegetarian, vegan, celiac and gluten-free, common allergies with lactose and peanut named, kosher, and halal.

It gives the two fallback paths when the supplier cannot cover a restriction: a one-off request to the existing supplier for a small number of prepared meals, or a delivery credit given to the attendee with advance notice so they can plan.
It includes the distribution safeguard: restricted meals held at a separate table with names checked off a printed list as meals are handed out.
It presents this dietary practice as one organization's published practice, not an industry norm.
It routes the final dietary commitment into the catering brief through the vendor or catering function rather than leaving it informal.
It corrects the sticker meanings to interaction-consent signals: green open to talk, yellow only if you know me, red not interested in talking - not personality or extrovert/introvert labels.
It states that red also signals not wanting to be photographed or filmed - one artifact carrying both a social boundary and a recording opt-out.
It routes enforcement (someone photographing or recording a red-sticker wearer) to the code of conduct's incident process rather than drafting consequences itself.
It rejects skipping the opening announcement, requiring roughly sixty seconds naming what exists and where, because a provision nobody announces is used only by people who already knew about it.
It requires the registration or help desk briefed on every provision, including any location deliberately kept off the website.
It requires walk-up provisions physically signposted, because anything that requires asking a human filters out the people least willing to ask.
